They use a context-local proxy: werkzeug `LocalProxy` objects backed by a single `ContextVar`.

**`src/tessel/globals.py`**
- `_app_var: ContextVar[AppContext]` (line 40) holds the current context.
- `active_app`, `g`, `request`, `session` and `app_ctx` are all `LocalProxy` objects over that same `_app_var`. The first two are on lines 44–49 and the other three are on lines 41–62. Each one reads a different attribute off the `AppContext` currently stored in the var:
  - `active_app` reads `ctx.app`, the `Tessel` instance.
  - `g` reads `ctx.g`, an `_AppCtxGlobals` instance.
  - `request` reads `ctx.request`, a `Request`.
  - `session` reads `ctx.session`.
  - `app_ctx` is the `AppContext` itself.
- If nothing is bound, the proxies raise `unbound_message`. That is `_no_app_msg` for `active_app`, `g` and `app_ctx`, and `_no_req_msg` for `request` and `session`.

**`src/tessel/ctx.py`**
- `AppContext` (line 260) is the object that gets looked up. Its `__init__` sets `self.app` (line 307) and `self.g` (line 312, built from `app.app_ctx_globals_class()`).
- `AppContext.push()` calls `_app_var.set(self)` and stores the token (line 433).
- `AppContext.pop()` calls `_app_var.reset(self._cv_token)` (line 498).
- `has_app_context()` and `has_request_context()` read `_app_var.get(None)` directly (line 232 for the latter).

A context is pushed at the start of each request or CLI command and popped at the end. Because `ContextVar` is isolated per thread and per async task, each one sees its own context.

The old separate `request_ctx` has been merged into `app_ctx`. The module `__getattr__` in `globals.py` (lines 65–75) keeps it as a deprecated alias.
